I guess this is a little less on the conversational side, but it's important. As of right now, I'm the only mod, but I'd like to talk with you guys about what you expect mods to do—and not to do. Alternatively: what have been some of the worst experiences you've had with the powers-that-be on the internet?
What role should a moderator play in his/her verse?

IMHO the mods main job is to block and remove spam. The secondary job is to enforce the rules, warning or blocking the violators. The tertiary job is to provide content to keep the subvoat is dying.

A mod is also responsible for a readable design and an informative sidebar. To make the decision of joining clear and easy for new users.
That was better said than what I came to say, the only tweak I would make would be to clarify the rules as those the community desires. The moderator is a servant of the community.

In my honest opinion, if there are rules that you wouldn't have guessed just from reading the name of the sub, they're doing it wrong. Moderation is not to impose their own standards on things, it's just an overseeing and making sure everything is running smoothly and nobody is blatantly pissing everybody else off.
If you're doing it right, it's almost as if you've done nothing at all.
Except for being a good contributor, especially to ensure the 'verse don't die.

Moderators are there to make the sub look cool, drive activity with their own submissions and comments, and to make sure the community is heard and that reasonable complaints are addressed. I also find it useful to find other mods with the same vision and add them to the team to democratize things a bit. It's actually pretty hard to be a mod, it's a lot easier with help. On reddit I added a bunch of mods who see things the way I do and that I can trust to do the right thing, and I really don't do much anymore. I made all the stylesheets and banners but I don't mind when they change them.

I think more than anything it's just wanting what's best for the community rather than using it as a platform to feel powerful and to feed your own ego. Sadly the latter is way more common.

The worst experience I ever had was in /r/yankees, where I got banned for asking why the subreddit looked way worse than the default. He had changed the link color to black so you couldn't even see links. I still to this day don't understand why he got upset and banned everybody for calling him on it.

Realistically, the most you can do is just post enough to make the place feel vibrant, but not too much that I unsubscribe because it's flooding my frontpage. I can't tell you how many tiny subs I wanted to support before they spammed me with 20 submissions a day. It's actually a pretty common occurrence and a pretty fatal mistake. Two or three good ones a day is more than enough.
Provide quality content. /v/uncensored is mine and you can read the one simple rule. Nothing illegal.
